name: Zoe Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills your usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach flute in two school groups, play in a local quintet and record woodwind parts when studios call. My music bachelor's helps me explain the notation, and I have enough years behind me to teach ordinary pupils well; I still practise before each concert.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Malik drives buses, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My musician pay is typical, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other music schools nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school that a faster room list is welcome, but the child with a shaky flute note still needs a teacher beside the music stand. Our monthly quintet date should go on much as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI tools and don't see a reason to start for a small saving. We have about four months of expenses saved, and Malik's bus wages cover groceries while my school contract covers most of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my Tuesday and Thursday flute groups and the signed quintet date next month. This week I'll ask the school for next term's paid hours in writing before we book the children's holiday club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about whether the school renews every teaching hour, even with four months saved. A little office software would not change the work I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a recording date moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio moved a flute recording in May, but the school fee covered our mortgage that month. I waited for the revised date without asking Malik for an extra route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about holiday club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger child we can decide on holiday club after the timetable arrives. The school usually renews my hours, but the holiday club wants a signed date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school director to show where the money saved on score writing and booking goes. I would ask her to put my rehearsal hours on the paid timetable. An email saying I am valued is not a paid rehearsal hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Copying parts and making practice sheets bring about a fifth of my pay. Software may take those hours, while families still book live lessons; losing a fifth would eat our reserve faster than we can fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the director for separate paid teaching and preparation hours in the next contract. In the first year of this shift, if preparation pay falls, I'll ask the civic orchestra about its advertised flute tutoring slot only if the audition accepts my bachelor's and net pay after travel and school pickup replaces the lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real cut to my own pay. Four months saved is enough to search, not a reason to accept unpaid preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that orchestra slot actually open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra posted a part-time tutor role in spring, but it has already closed. I would ask for the next notice rather than count it as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the school for a volunteer title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current pupils while auditioning. If the orchestra offers only a volunteer title, I would stay where I am until paid terms are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my pupils that full AGI by 2028 can prepare a flute part cheaply, but it does not sign a school teaching contract for me. I would keep the quintet rehearsing for paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could write parts, plan lessons and answer families more cheaply than I can. Robots able to play hands-on music arrive around 2031; the live quintet may last longer, but the fifth of my pay from preparation could disappear first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the school for a 2028 hours plan and list what each teaching, preparation and quintet date paid last year. In the first year after 2028, if a teaching afternoon is also cut, I'll apply for a posted instrumental tutor role at another school only if my bachelor's meets its rules and written net pay after travel covers the lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than defeated, because Malik's wage and four months saved give me a short search. Losing paid preparation would still tighten the mortgage every month. Four months saved buys time for an audition, not a new monthly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are those nearby tutor posts available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two schools nearby hired tutors last year, but neither has offered me anything. I would check the new vacancy's teaching hours against the children's pickup before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you call the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my reserve falls below two months while the school cuts a day, I would ask the lender about a temporary mortgage change. Malik and I would get the full extra interest in writing before agreeing.

transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quintet five years lets us build a paid local audience instead of counting on sheet-copying fees. I would try a small chamber session only if families put money down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take parts and lesson plans, with robots able to play around 2034. Easy score work may fade before full AGI, so the longer warning still puts my own pay at risk while we have a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask the public library about a monthly family chamber session, but only if it gives us a room, four players have signed fees and nine families prepay enough to cover everyone. In the first year after 2031, I'll keep the session only if nine families return and the library renews the room terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the score fees fading early. A small paid session gives us something to test without borrowing from the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the library actually have a room for your group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library has held concerts before, but it has not offered our quintet the room. I would ask the librarian for an actual date and the insurance cost before taking deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if deposits do not cover players and insurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nine deposits don't cover the players' quoted fees and insurance, I'll refund them and keep our regular dates. I would ask the players to hold a date only after the money clears. Four players cannot practise on a promise that nine families might pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school a decade gives us time to secure paid teaching that survives changes in score software. I would still give children a flute in their hands and teach them to hear one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, I still have a mortgage and years of work ahead. Robots around 2039 could play too, while easy copying fees may vanish earlier; I need stable school hours rather than a promise about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask two school districts about music-teacher certification and enrol only if a grant covers fees, my bachelor's meets entry rules and Malik can handle the children's evenings. By 2036 I'll aim for six months of expenses saved from spare paid lesson fees after household bills; in the first year after AGI, I'll take a posted school teaching role only if its written net offer after travel covers the mortgage and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because copy work could fade before 2036, even with time for a course. Our four-month reserve is for the children and mortgage, not for tuition a district might reject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the certificate counts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check that both districts accept the course before registering. If one will not, I can still ask the other, but I will not pay for a certificate neither accepts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave your current school hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my existing school pupils until a new district signs real paid hours. We would check pickup and travel before accepting those hours. An interview cannot pay the mortgage while I wait for a school contract.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because preparation fees could stop before I know whether school teaching hours hold. A written hours plan, an actual qualifying vacancy and full lender costs if a day is cut would give us choices before missing the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a library concert pays the players before it pays me. I will not ask four people to rehearse on a promise of ticket sales.

headlineQuote: I will not ask four people to rehearse on a promise of ticket sales.
portrait: Zoe is a **43-year-old** experienced flute teacher with a music bachelor's, school groups, quintet dates and recording work.
She has **four months saved**, typical pay, two children and a mortgage, with some nearby music schools.
She never uses **AI tools** and expects paid notation and preparation work to shrink before robot players arrive.
She seeks **written school hours**, qualifying vacancies, funded certification and fully paid player fees before new work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because preparation pay may stop before school hours are settled.
whatWouldHelp: A **written hours plan**, real tutor vacancy and clear lender costs would protect the mortgage while she adjusts.
